prose.heroLede: I build AI-ready design systems with 1:1 code parity and architect the AI workflows that connect product, design, and engineering. Working alongside Technical Product Managers and developers, I help eliminate the traditional handoff by designing systems, optimising processes, and contributing directly to PRDs, prototypes, and production code.
prose.cvSummary: I build AI-ready design systems: component libraries with 1:1 parity between Figma and code, plus custom Claude skills and MCP setups that let agents assemble UI from the real system without drift. I write and ship the frontend myself, reviewed and merged by engineering. Under the tooling sits seven years of research practice — user interviews, usability testing, and WCAG 2.1 AA auditing.

background.prose: Before tech, I spent eleven years helping build and grow a strength and nutrition coaching practice. As the owner's close business partner, I took ownership of many of the systems that defined the business. I led a team of coaches, designed the recruitment and onboarding programme, created the assessment framework used across the practice, conducted hundreds of client interviews, and built a data-driven approach to measuring progress and outcomes.
background.statement: It taught me something design school doesn't: people rarely behave the way they say they will. You have to meet them where they are and design not for what they say, not even what they think they want, but for what they truly need at that moment in their journey.

openSource: Tokens are born in the repo, not in Figma. One tokens.json builds the site's CSS variables and a flat JSON that both AI agents and a one-way repo-to-Figma push read — which makes Figma an output of the system rather than its source. Every component ships as a CSS block, a machine-readable spec for agents, and a Storybook story, and the build fails if any of the three is missing, so parity is enforced rather than maintained by hand.
Light and dark come from the same token file: a themed colour carries its dark value beside its light one, and the entire theme is 24 re-aliased tokens with zero per-component rules.

projects.summary: An AI-ready design system that ships itself: repo-first tokens, Storybook, one-way Figma push, auto-deploys — all open source.
projects.subtitle: Every claim on this page is inspectable in the same public repository that renders it. If the system were not real, this page could not exist in the shape it does.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A designer's portfolio usually describes process. This one demonstrates it: every button, chip, and square on this page comes from a design system that lives in the same public repository, documents itself for AI agents, and ships automatically. If I claim to build AI-ready systems, the claim should be inspectable.

sections.heading: The system
sections.text: Repo-first tokens. One JSON file is the only place a colour is born. A zero-dependency script generates the CSS variables this very page loads, plus a machine-readable flat file for AI agents and the Figma push. Every component is three things. A CSS block, an AI spec (canonical HTML pattern + do/don't rules), and a Storybook story. The build fails if any of the three is missing — governance as a 90-line script, not a platform. The skeleton is the concept. A 24-square sheet whose rails are real square divs sized by the layout's own fr-tracks — and Conway's Game of Life lives on them. Click a square: the life you seed is born blueprint-blue and its lineage fades to stone.

sections.heading: The pipeline
sections.text: GitHub → Vercel. Two deployments from one public repo: this site (pure static, no build) and the Storybook, rebuilt on every push to main. Repo → Figma. Tokens flow one way — an AI agent pushes them as Figma Variables following a written, idempotent procedure. Figma is an output, never a source. Repo → AI. CLAUDE.md routes any agent to the system's README and per-component specs; an agent can assemble correct UI from the canonical patterns without seeing the site first.

sections.heading: Receipts
sections.text: 0 accessibility violations across the component library — axe-audited per story, WCAG 2.1 AA contrast decisions documented inside the tokens themselves, and verified in both themes. 84 tokens, 149 values, 21 components — one token carries its light, dark and print values together; each component is enforced as CSS + AI spec + story by the build. Dark mode is 24 tokens and zero component rules. A themed colour carries its dark value beside its light one; the build emits the media query and the pinned-theme override. There is no prefers-color-scheme anywhere in the component CSS — the sharpest test a semantic token layer can be put to. No build step in the site. Two link tags consume the system; view-source shows everything.

projects.title: AI-ready design systems and Agentic workflows

projects.subtitle: Infrastructure that lets AI generate production-faithful UI: 1:1 Figma-to-code parity, custom Claude skills, and a prototype pipeline for the whole TPM team.

sections.heading: The problem
sections.text: Green Street is a leading commercial real estate data and analytics company. I was brought in to redesign the AI Assistant module, and found that PM wireframes, design files, and coded components lived in separate worlds — a component could look one way in Figma and behave completely differently in production. Fragmented handoff. No enforced relationship between mockups, design, and code. AI couldn't read the system. Every AI-generated UI drifted from the actual components. No prototype pipeline. TPMs pulled design resources into every minor exploration.

sections.heading: The approach
sections.text: Audit and architecture. A full audit of the component landscape — duplication, inconsistency, missing states, accessibility failures — then a token-first architecture with semantic naming. Every component exposes its full range of states, so AI and developers never need to guess. 1:1 Figma-to-code parity. A Figma library of ~35 components and growing, each mapping exactly to a coded component: same name, same props, same variants. I drove the alignment with engineering — attending standups and reviewing implementations to catch drift early. Tokens in the frontend, not just the design file. I implemented the tokens directly in the frontend component library, replacing every hardcoded value for 100% token coverage across the module. A design system that only exists in Figma is a picture of a design system. A living style guide. Every token and every component, rendered from the real implementation — used for visual regression testing and for design-to-code comparison, so drift is something you can see rather than something you discover in review. Custom Claude skills. A persistent knowledge layer that teaches Claude to read the token structure, assemble the correct native components, respect spacing and hierarchy, and generate prototypes faithful to the real system. No drift. No invented components. TPM prototype pipeline. A PM describes a screen; the pipeline assembles a working interactive prototype from real system components. The feedback loop between product thinking and validated interaction went from days to minutes.

sections.heading: Shipping production code
sections.text: I authored the complete responsive navigation component for the Green Street Analytics platform — built with Claude Code guided by the custom skills, reviewed and approved by the engineering team, and live in production. Not a prototype: production frontend code serving real users.

sections.heading: Outcomes
sections.text: TPMs generate accurate prototypes without design involvement in every cycle. A single source of truth between Figma and code — translation ambiguity eliminated. Every new component added becomes immediately AI-accessible. A design-to-code pipeline in progress: from Figma screen to reviewed frontend implementation. This work sits at the intersection of deep Figma craft, frontend architecture, and applied AI expertise — not using off-the-shelf tools, but building the tools themselves.

projects.title: UX & Accessibility Audits
projects.summary: WCAG 2.1 AA audits of two product surfaces — editorial and data-dense analytics. 200+ issue instances catalogued with severity ratings and a prioritised remediation roadmap.
projects.subtitle: End-to-end WCAG 2.1 AA audits of two distinct product surfaces — an editorial platform and a data-dense analytics platform — with severity-rated, annotated remediation roadmaps.

sections.heading: Why it matters here
sections.text: Green Street's users are professional analysts, investors, and brokers making high-stakes financial decisions — many across multiple screens for hours, some with assistive technologies. For a data company, an unlabelled filter or a contrast failure isn't just an accessibility issue. It's a credibility gap.

sections.heading: Green Street News — editorial
sections.text: Colour contrast — systematic review against WCAG 2.1 AA thresholds across article bodies, bylines, timestamps, and navigation. Semantic structure — heading hierarchy that means something to a screen reader, not just visually. Keyboard navigation — focus traps, missing indicators, mouse-only elements. Labelling — icon-only buttons, ambiguous "read more" links, unlabelled form controls.

sections.heading: Analytics & Research Platform — data-dense
sections.text: Data tables — header scope, captions, sortable column accessibility, nested headers. Charts — text alternatives, colour-only encoding, keyboard-accessible data views. Filters & faceted search — keyboard operability, focus management, live region announcements. Dynamic content — explicit focus management for async loading, panels, and modals. Full AA sweep — criterion-by-criterion review of all 50 AA success criteria.

sections.heading: Deliverables
sections.text: Issue instances catalogued across the two surfaces. Every finding documented with a severity rating (Critical / Major / Minor), WCAG criterion reference, annotated screenshot, recommended fix, and estimated engineering effort — plus a mapping to the platform workflow it affects, so engineering unblocks the most-used analytical paths first. The output is a prioritised remediation roadmap, not a list of complaints.

sections.heading: Outcomes
sections.text: Both products now have a clear, actionable roadmap to WCAG 2.1 AA compliance. Cross-product observations shaped component prioritisation in the AI-ready design system — the most inconsistent patterns became the first to be standardised. A repeatable audit methodology for every new product surface as the platform grows.

projects.title: Cleaning Service Marketplace

metrics.label: reduction in front page bounce rate

projects.summary: Multi-year, research-led UX. Front page, flows, onboarding, loyalty — bounce rate down 40%, retention up.
projects.subtitle: A research-led, multi-year UX engagement on Bulgaria's leading cleaning services marketplace — every design change grounded in evidence, not assumption.

sections.heading: The brief
sections.text: Three user types, three definitions of success: clients booking a service and deciding who to trust, service providers competing on reputation, and housemaids needing a low-friction onboarding path. The challenge: serve all three without making any of them feel second-class.

sections.heading: Research
sections.text: Competitor analysis showed Domestina had no direct comprehensive competitor in the Bulgarian market — it had to define its own UX standards. Personas built from interviews, support tickets, Google Analytics, and Hotjar surfaced the critical insight: clients were anxious about inviting a stranger into their home. Trust signals weren't nice-to-haves — they were the primary conversion driver.

sections.heading: What I changed
sections.text: Front page redesign — restructured around the primary client action, trust signals moved above the fold, provider recruitment split into its own entry point. Domestina Club — loyalty mechanics designed into existing flows without adding friction to conversion. Provider workshops — made performance feedback clear and actionable, improving the whole provider pool. Housemaid registration — progressive disclosure with named stages and visible momentum.

sections.heading: Measured outcomes
sections.text: 40% reduction in front page bounce rate — from a focused hierarchy redesign, not a full rebuild. Marked increase in completed housemaid registrations. Improved retention following the Domestina Club launch. Stronger provider performance after workshop-driven design changes. Not a single project — a continuous improvement methodology applied to a live, growing marketplace over multiple years.

projects.title: Municipal Mobile App
projects.summary: Civic app serving tourists and older residents at once. White-label token system. Live on the App Store and Google Play.
projects.subtitle: End-to-end design of a cross-platform civic app serving two opposing audiences — tourists and older residents — live on the App Store and Google Play.

sections.heading: The challenge
sections.text: Two audiences with almost opposing needs. Tourists are explorers — visual richness, maps, discovery flows. Local residents, many of them older, need municipal services: waste schedules, announcements, contacts — with large touch targets, minimal cognitive load, and zero ambiguity.

sections.heading: The dual colour logic
sections.text: Green encodes everything tourism — nature reserves, trails, gastronomy — connecting to the Strandzha region's identity. Blue encodes everything administrative, carrying the institutional calm of government services. This is not decoration; it's a wayfinding system. A user glancing at a card knows instantly whether it's a tourist recommendation or a municipal service — before reading a word. For older users, colour becomes a cognitive shortcut.

sections.heading: White-label design system
sections.text: Semantic colour tokens — swap the green/blue for any municipality's brand and it cascades through the entire system. Spacing and rounding tokens — no arbitrary values anywhere in the library. Typography system — Comfortaa, tokenised scale, friendly yet official. Icon system — municipal logo redesigned on a 64×80 grid, coherent from app icon to in-app header.

sections.heading: Accessibility by default
sections.text: Touch targets exceeding WCAG's 44×44px minimum throughout. WCAG 2.1 AA contrast across both colour contexts. Hierarchy through size, weight, and spacing — never colour alone. Progressive disclosure for dense municipal content.

sections.heading: Outcomes
sections.text: Launched on iOS and Android, publicly available on both stores. The white-label system is a reusable product — any Bulgarian municipality can deploy it with brand-token changes alone. The dual colour logic became a reference model for designing civic services for mixed-age audiences.

components.a11y: Use <a> to navigate and <button> to act; the global :focus-visible ring is never suppressed.
Titles are <h3> inside a section headed by <h2> — the heading order is the contract.
Thread is role=log aria-live=polite; the composer keeps focus while busy (aria-disabled + readOnly, never the disabled attribute).
Display-only <span>. Anything that responds to a click is a Button instead.
role=dialog aria-modal=true labelled by its title; the focus trap and focus restore are mandatory.
role=dialog aria-modal=true labelled by its title; the focus trap, Escape and focus restore are mandatory, and the opener carries aria-expanded.
Role is <h3> under the section <h2>; bullet glyphs are ::before so the list is still announced as a list.
All three parts are required — a number with no label is unreadable; the counter degrades to plain text without JS or with reduced motion.
The only inverse surface on the page; its label token is rated against that surface in both themes.
External links carry target=_blank rel=noopener and a trailing arrow; labels name the destination, never 'click here'.
Every real needs meaningful alt text describing the content, never 'screenshot'.
<nav aria-label="Primary">; the status dot is aria-hidden and hover states hold AA contrast.
Real <dl>/<dt>/<dd> semantics, each pair wrapped in a <div> for the grid.
Project rows are <button>s; .idx__go is aria-hidden because the whole row is the target.
Always an <h2>; the note is hidden under 640px, so it may never carry essential information.
Rails and strips are decoration: js/automata.js sets aria-hidden on every one, its canvas carries none of the page's meaning, and content never goes in them.
Real <ol>/<li>; the ordinal is content inside the item, not a CSS counter a screen reader would skip.
A framed number inside prose — it adds no semantics, so the sentence around it has to still read correctly.
Pure decoration: it carries aria-hidden, holds no content and is never focusable or announced — its only job is to be the height nobody's words are using.
A real <button> with three states, so no aria-pressed; the aria-label carries the current state and what activating does.
Display levels are uppercased by CSS, so source text stays normal case and is announced as words rather than letters.

evalsPage.$doc: Hand-authored prose for evals.html section 04. Placeholders are filled by evals/run.mjs. Not chunked, not in the manifest: changing it moves neither the vector corpus hash nor corpus.manifestChars.

html: Plain lexical search won on ranking, and the structured arm lost. BM25 reaches {{evals:bm25.hit3}} hit@3 and {{evals:bm25.mrr}} MRR; navigating by name reaches {{evals:tools-only.hit3}} and {{evals:tools-only.mrr}}. The design being evaluated here expected the opposite, and the number is reported the way it came out. The reason is visible in the failures: a name match fires on whichever entity happens to share a word with the question, and on questions phrased the way people actually phrase them — “what user research methods does he use?” — no entity is named at all. The corpus is small, single-author and lexically consistent, which is precisely the condition under which BM25 is strong.

Knowing when to say nothing is where they separate, and it is not close. BM25 abstains on {{evals:bm25.abstained}} of {{evals:abstention.total}} unanswerable questions. It returns a confident ranked list for “did he ever work at Google?” — the word appears eight times in the corpus, in Google Analytics, Google Play and Google AI Studio, none of them an employer — and for “what are his salary expectations?”, and for “does he speak Japanese?”. The tools arm abstains on {{evals:tools-only.abstained}} of {{evals:abstention.total}}, because no entity was named. That is not a tuning artefact; it is the difference between matching words and resolving identifiers.

Fusing the two rankings made both worse. Tools-first with BM25 appended scores {{evals:hybrid.hit3}} hit@3 — below BM25 alone — and abstains on nothing, because the fallback always fires. It inherits the weaker ranking and the weaker judgement. That result killed the originally proposed shape, which is the most useful thing this table did.

What the failure suggested instead. Stop fusing rankings and split responsibilities: let the name match decide whether the corpus covers the question, and let BM25 decide what comes back once it does. That arm — tools-gated — holds {{evals:tools-gated.hit3}} hit@3 and {{evals:tools-gated.separability}} separability, tied for best in the table, while raising the abstention rate to {{evals:tools-gated.abstain}}. Roughly seven points of ranking traded for the entire ability to say “not on file”. It is labelled post-hoc everywhere it appears, because it was written after seeing the first three arms on this same question set; it is a hypothesis this run suggests, not a result this run establishes, and it needs questions written after it to become one.

Two holes in the corpus, found by the eval rather than by a reviewer. Location, availability and contact details live in content.json as structured fields and appear in no chunk, so “where is he based?” cannot be answered by any search over prose — the only chunk containing the word “Sofia” is the education line, about Sofia University, and BM25 duly returns something else entirely. Separately, the 2007–2009 quality assurance role has no bullet points, so the content build produced no chunk for it at all: the role is in the index and invisible to search, and every arm scores zero on it. Both are why the tool layer reads structured fields directly instead of searching for them.

One question no arm could answer, and it is the case for embeddings. “How far has he run?” shares no term with “42 km. Marathon finisher.” — lexical search returns nothing at all. That is the exact shape of question a semantic retriever exists for. The embeddings arm has since been run: it answers this question and wins every retrieval class, at {{evals:embeddings.hit3}} hit@3 against BM25's {{evals:bm25.hit3}}. The argument became a measurement.

The point the corpus statistics make on their own. The complete table of contents — every project id, title, client, tag and one-line summary, every role and span — is a few thousand characters. It fits in the system prompt. A retriever exists to solve “I cannot enumerate what is in here”; when the whole index fits in the prompt, that problem does not exist, and provisioning a stateful, billed service to solve it anyway is a decision about a résumé rather than about a corpus. That argument survives this table. The claim that structured lookup also ranks better did not.

review.now: OPEN, and wrong twice over. BM25 gained a stopword list, so it now holds 83.7% hit@3 against tools-gated's 34.7% — the trade is 49 points, not seven. And BM25 now abstains on 43.8% of the unanswerable questions by itself, because a query made only of function words yields no scoring term, so tools-gated no longer confers "the entire ability" to abstain.
review.cannotInterpolate: "seven points" is a difference between two cells and "the entire ability" is a claim about one arm having none of a capability; neither is a metric this file can carry as a placeholder without a new formatter
review.resolution: OPEN — needs the owner. Both figures exist as placeholders already ({{evals:tools-gated.hit3}} and {{evals:bm25.hit3}}), so a wording that states the two numbers instead of their difference would be re-run-proof — but choosing that wording is authoring, not interpolation.

review.phrase: and for “what are his salary expectations?”, and for “does he speak Japanese?”
review.was: true when BM25 had no stopword list and scored on any query term at all
review.now: OPEN. Both questions now tokenise to content words only — [salary, expectations] and [speak, japanese] — none of which appears in the corpus, so BM25 returns NOTHING for both. They are now examples of the opposite of what the sentence uses them for. The third example survives: “did he ever work at Google?” still returns eight results, because `google` is genuinely in the corpus nine times.
review.cannotInterpolate: the sentence names specific questions and asserts a behaviour for them; no placeholder can carry a worked example
review.resolution: OPEN — needs the owner. Caused by the stopword list, which is a retrieval improvement (+16pp hit@3) that made two of this paragraph's three illustrations obsolete. Reported rather than rewritten. Whichever examples replace them should be chosen from the seven questions BM25 still answers confidently, which evals/results.json lists.

review.phrase: the word appears eight times in the corpus, in Google Analytics, Google Play and Google AI Studio, none of them an employer
review.now: OPEN, and independent of the stopword change: `google` occurs 10 times across 9 chunks (df=9). The reasoning is untouched — none of the occurrences is an employer — only the count is stale.
review.cannotInterpolate: a corpus term frequency is interpolatable in principle, but there is no placeholder source for one today; adding a `term` source would make this class of claim safe permanently
review.resolution: OPEN — needs the owner for the wording, though this one is a plain figure correction rather than a judgement. Worth noting as the argument for a `{{evals:term.google.count}}`-style placeholder source: this is the only figure in the prose that no gate can currently reach.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Multi-year, research-led UX. Front page, flows, onboarding, loyalty — bounce rate down 40%, retention up.

chunks.heading: Subtitle
chunks.text: A research-led, multi-year UX engagement on Bulgaria's leading cleaning services marketplace — every design change grounded in evidence, not assumption.

chunks.heading: The brief
chunks.text: Three user types, three definitions of success: clients booking a service and deciding who to trust, service providers competing on reputation, and housemaids needing a low-friction onboarding path. The challenge: serve all three without making any of them feel second-class.

chunks.heading: Research
chunks.text: Competitor analysis showed Domestina had no direct comprehensive competitor in the Bulgarian market — it had to define its own UX standards. Personas built from interviews, support tickets, Google Analytics, and Hotjar surfaced the critical insight: clients were anxious about inviting a stranger into their home. Trust signals weren't nice-to-haves — they were the primary conversion driver.

chunks.heading: What I changed
chunks.text: Front page redesign — restructured around the primary client action, trust signals moved above the fold, provider recruitment split into its own entry point. Domestina Club — loyalty mechanics designed into existing flows without adding friction to conversion. Provider workshops — made performance feedback clear and actionable, improving the whole provider pool. Housemaid registration — progressive disclosure with named stages and visible momentum.

chunks.heading: Measured outcomes
chunks.text: 40% reduction in front page bounce rate — from a focused hierarchy redesign, not a full rebuild. Marked increase in completed housemaid registrations. Improved retention following the Domestina Club launch. Stronger provider performance after workshop-driven design changes. Not a single project — a continuous improvement methodology applied to a live, growing marketplace over multiple years.

chunks.heading: Subtitle
chunks.text: End-to-end WCAG 2.1 AA audits of two distinct product surfaces — an editorial platform and a data-dense analytics platform — with severity-rated, annotated remediation roadmaps.

chunks.heading: Why it matters here
chunks.text: Green Street's users are professional analysts, investors, and brokers making high-stakes financial decisions — many across multiple screens for hours, some with assistive technologies. For a data company, an unlabelled filter or a contrast failure isn't just an accessibility issue. It's a credibility gap.

chunks.heading: Green Street News — editorial
chunks.text: Colour contrast — systematic review against WCAG 2.1 AA thresholds across article bodies, bylines, timestamps, and navigation. Semantic structure — heading hierarchy that means something to a screen reader, not just visually. Keyboard navigation — focus traps, missing indicators, mouse-only elements. Labelling — icon-only buttons, ambiguous "read more" links, unlabelled form controls.

chunks.heading: Analytics & Research Platform — data-dense
chunks.text: Data tables — header scope, captions, sortable column accessibility, nested headers. Charts — text alternatives, colour-only encoding, keyboard-accessible data views. Filters & faceted search — keyboard operability, focus management, live region announcements. Dynamic content — explicit focus management for async loading, panels, and modals. Full AA sweep — criterion-by-criterion review of all 50 AA success criteria.

chunks.heading: Deliverables
chunks.text: Issue instances catalogued across the two surfaces. Every finding documented with a severity rating (Critical / Major / Minor), WCAG criterion reference, annotated screenshot, recommended fix, and estimated engineering effort — plus a mapping to the platform workflow it affects, so engineering unblocks the most-used analytical paths first. The output is a prioritised remediation roadmap, not a list of complaints.

chunks.heading: Outcomes
chunks.text: Both products now have a clear, actionable roadmap to WCAG 2.1 AA compliance. Cross-product observations shaped component prioritisation in the AI-ready design system — the most inconsistent patterns became the first to be standardised. A repeatable audit methodology for every new product surface as the platform grows.

cite.label: Green Street — AI-ready design systems and Agentic workflows

chunks.heading: The problem
chunks.text: Green Street is a leading commercial real estate data and analytics company. I was brought in to redesign the AI Assistant module, and found that PM wireframes, design files, and coded components lived in separate worlds — a component could look one way in Figma and behave completely differently in production. Fragmented handoff. No enforced relationship between mockups, design, and code. AI couldn't read the system. Every AI-generated UI drifted from the actual components. No prototype pipeline. TPMs pulled design resources into every minor exploration.

cite.label: Green Street — AI-ready design systems and Agentic workflows

chunks.heading: The approach
chunks.text: Audit and architecture. A full audit of the component landscape — duplication, inconsistency, missing states, accessibility failures — then a token-first architecture with semantic naming. Every component exposes its full range of states, so AI and developers never need to guess. 1:1 Figma-to-code parity. A Figma library of ~35 components and growing, each mapping exactly to a coded component: same name, same props, same variants. I drove the alignment with engineering — attending standups and reviewing implementations to catch drift early. Tokens in the frontend, not just the design file. I implemented the tokens directly in the frontend component library, replacing every hardcoded value for 100% token coverage across the module. A design system that only exists in Figma is a picture of a design system. A living style guide. Every token and every component, rendered from the real implementation — used for visual regression testing and for design-to-code comparison, so drift is something you can see rather than something you discover in review. Custom Claude skills. A persistent knowledge layer that teaches Claude to read the token structure, assemble the correct native components, respect spacing and hierarchy, and generate prototypes faithful to the real system. No drift. No invented components. TPM prototype pipeline. A PM describes a screen; the pipeline assembles a working interactive prototype from real system components. The feedback loop between product thinking and validated interaction went from days to minutes.

cite.label: Green Street — AI-ready design systems and Agentic workflows

chunks.heading: Shipping production code
chunks.text: I authored the complete responsive navigation component for the Green Street Analytics platform — built with Claude Code guided by the custom skills, reviewed and approved by the engineering team, and live in production. Not a prototype: production frontend code serving real users.

cite.label: Green Street — AI-ready design systems and Agentic workflows

chunks.heading: Outcomes
chunks.text: TPMs generate accurate prototypes without design involvement in every cycle. A single source of truth between Figma and code — translation ambiguity eliminated. Every new component added becomes immediately AI-accessible. A design-to-code pipeline in progress: from Figma screen to reviewed frontend implementation. This work sits at the intersection of deep Figma craft, frontend architecture, and applied AI expertise — not using off-the-shelf tools, but building the tools themselves.

chunks.heading: The challenge
chunks.text: Two audiences with almost opposing needs. Tourists are explorers — visual richness, maps, discovery flows. Local residents, many of them older, need municipal services: waste schedules, announcements, contacts — with large touch targets, minimal cognitive load, and zero ambiguity.

cite.label: Municipality of Malko Tarnovo — Municipal Mobile App

chunks.heading: The dual colour logic
chunks.text: Green encodes everything tourism — nature reserves, trails, gastronomy — connecting to the Strandzha region's identity. Blue encodes everything administrative, carrying the institutional calm of government services. This is not decoration; it's a wayfinding system. A user glancing at a card knows instantly whether it's a tourist recommendation or a municipal service — before reading a word. For older users, colour becomes a cognitive shortcut.

cite.label: Municipality of Malko Tarnovo — Municipal Mobile App

chunks.heading: White-label design system
chunks.text: Semantic colour tokens — swap the green/blue for any municipality's brand and it cascades through the entire system. Spacing and rounding tokens — no arbitrary values anywhere in the library. Typography system — Comfortaa, tokenised scale, friendly yet official. Icon system — municipal logo redesigned on a 64×80 grid, coherent from app icon to in-app header.

cite.label: Municipality of Malko Tarnovo — Municipal Mobile App

chunks.heading: Accessibility by default
chunks.text: Touch targets exceeding WCAG's 44×44px minimum throughout. WCAG 2.1 AA contrast across both colour contexts. Hierarchy through size, weight, and spacing — never colour alone. Progressive disclosure for dense municipal content.

cite.label: Municipality of Malko Tarnovo — Municipal Mobile App

chunks.heading: Outcomes
chunks.text: Launched on iOS and Android, publicly available on both stores. The white-label system is a reusable product — any Bulgarian municipality can deploy it with brand-token changes alone. The dual colour logic became a reference model for designing civic services for mixed-age audiences.

cite.label: This site — Portfolio as a Product

chunks.heading: The idea
chunks.text: A designer's portfolio usually describes process. This one demonstrates it: every button, chip, and square on this page comes from a design system that lives in the same public repository, documents itself for AI agents, and ships automatically. If I claim to build AI-ready systems, the claim should be inspectable.

cite.label: This site — Portfolio as a Product

chunks.heading: The system
chunks.text: Repo-first tokens. One JSON file is the only place a colour is born. A zero-dependency script generates the CSS variables this very page loads, plus a machine-readable flat file for AI agents and the Figma push. Every component is three things. A CSS block, an AI spec (canonical HTML pattern + do/don't rules), and a Storybook story. The build fails if any of the three is missing — governance as a 90-line script, not a platform. The skeleton is the concept. A 24-square sheet whose rails are real square divs sized by the layout's own fr-tracks — and Conway's Game of Life lives on them. Click a square: the life you seed is born blueprint-blue and its lineage fades to stone.

cite.label: This site — Portfolio as a Product

chunks.heading: The pipeline
chunks.text: GitHub → Vercel. Two deployments from one public repo: this site (pure static, no build) and the Storybook, rebuilt on every push to main. Repo → Figma. Tokens flow one way — an AI agent pushes them as Figma Variables following a written, idempotent procedure. Figma is an output, never a source. Repo → AI. CLAUDE.md routes any agent to the system's README and per-component specs; an agent can assemble correct UI from the canonical patterns without seeing the site first.

cite.label: This site — Portfolio as a Product

chunks.heading: Receipts
chunks.text: 0 accessibility violations across the component library — axe-audited per story, WCAG 2.1 AA contrast decisions documented inside the tokens themselves, and verified in both themes. tokens, values, components — one token carries its light, dark and print values together; each component is enforced as CSS + AI spec + story by the build. Dark mode is tokens and zero component rules. A themed colour carries its dark value beside its light one; the build emits the media query and the pinned-theme override. There is no prefers-color-scheme anywhere in the component CSS — the sharpest test a semantic token layer can be put to. No build step in the site. Two link tags consume the system; view-source shows everything.
